title: Corals and their partners
paras: Reef-building corals owe much of their success to a partnership that is invisible to the casual observer.
Living within the tissues of most such corals are single-celled algae called zooxanthellae, which photosynthesize and pass as much as ninety percent of the sugars they produce to their hosts.
In return, the coral supplies the algae with shelter and with nitrogen and carbon dioxide, waste products of its own metabolism.
This exchange allows corals to flourish in tropical waters that are notably poor in nutrients.
Yet the arrangement is fragile.
When water temperatures rise even one or two degrees above the usual summer maximum for several weeks, the algae begin to produce toxic compounds, and the coral expels them.
Stripped of its partners, the coral turns white, a phenomenon known as bleaching, and unless the algae return, it may starve.

questions.prompt: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.t: comparing the metabolism of corals with that of algae
options.why: There is no comparison of metabolisms.

options.t: describing a mutually beneficial relationship and a circumstance that disrupts it
options.why: Covers both halves: the exchange, then the bleaching that breaks it.

options.t: questioning the claim that corals depend on algae for food
options.why: The passage affirms that dependence.

options.t: arguing that rising temperatures will destroy most coral reefs
options.why: The passage makes no prediction about most reefs.

options.t: explaining why tropical waters are poor in nutrients
options.why: Nutrient-poor water is mentioned only once, as background.

questions.explain: The passage has two parts joined by "Yet the arrangement is fragile." A main-idea answer must cover both the partnership and its breakdown.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred from the passage that a coral that has bleached

options.t: has lost access to most of the sugars it normally receives
options.why: The algae supplied up to ninety percent of the sugars, and they have been expelled.

options.t: produces toxic compounds that harm nearby algae
options.why: It is the algae, not the coral, that produce the toxic compounds.

options.t: will recover once the water temperature drops
options.why: The passage gives no guarantee of recovery.

options.t: has already died
options.why: The passage says it "may starve" unless the algae return, so it is not yet dead.

options.t: can no longer supply nitrogen to its environment
options.why: The passage never discusses this.

questions.explain: Combine two facts: the algae provide most of the coral's sugars, and bleaching means the algae are gone. The inference follows with no extra assumption.

questions.prompt: Select the sentence that explains why the partnership is especially valuable in the corals' particular habitat.
questions.explain: The key phrase is "particular habitat." Only this sentence connects the partnership to the nutrient-poor tropical waters where corals live.

title: The paint tube and Impressionism
paras: Histories of Impressionism often credit the movement's innovations to a new way of seeing, but a humbler invention deserves some of the praise.
Until the 1840s, painters who wished to work outdoors had to grind their own pigments and store them in pig bladders, which burst easily and could not be resealed.
The collapsible metal paint tube, patented in 1841 by the American painter John Goffe Rand, made premixed colors portable and durable.
Renoir reportedly remarked that without tubes there would have been no Impressionism.
The claim is surely exaggerated: painters had sketched outdoors long before, and the Impressionists' interest in fleeting light grew out of debates within French painting itself.
Still, the tube turned outdoor painting from an arduous exception into an ordinary practice, and in doing so it made the Impressionists' ambitions practical.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.t: trace the history of the pigments used by the Impressionists
options.why: Pigments themselves are not traced.

options.t: defend Renoir's view of the importance of the paint tube
options.why: The author calls Renoir's claim "surely exaggerated."

options.t: refute the claim that Impressionism grew out of debates within French painting
options.why: The author accepts that claim.

options.t: explain why painters before the 1840s did not paint outdoors
options.why: The passage says they did sketch outdoors.

options.t: argue that a technological change deserves partial credit for an artistic movement
options.why: "Deserves some of the praise" and the final "Still..." sentence make exactly this argument.

questions.explain: Watch the word "partial." The author gives the tube some credit but not all of it, and the right answer keeps that moderate position.

questions.prompt: The author's attitude toward Renoir's remark can best be described as

options.t: amused indifference
options.why: The author engages seriously with the remark.

options.t: qualified acceptance
options.why: The author rejects its strong form but, with "Still," grants that the tube mattered.

options.t: complete dismissal
options.why: The author keeps part of Renoir's point.

options.t: puzzled uncertainty
options.why: The author takes a clear position.

options.t: wholehearted agreement
options.why: The author calls the remark exaggerated.

questions.explain: GRE authors are rarely extreme. "Surely exaggerated" followed by "Still" is the classic sign of a qualified view.

questions.prompt: Which of the following can be inferred about painters who worked before the 1840s?

options.t: Some of them painted or sketched outdoors, though doing so was difficult.
options.why: "Sketched outdoors long before" and "arduous exception" support this.

options.t: Some of them stored paint in containers that could not be resealed.
options.why: Pig bladders "could not be resealed."

options.t: They were uninterested in the effects of light.
options.why: Nothing in the passage supports this.

questions.explain: For "select all" questions, judge each choice on its own. Two choices are directly supported; the third goes beyond the passage.

title: What we own
paras: Standard economic theory assumes that the value a person places on an object does not depend on whether he or she already owns it.
Experiments suggest otherwise.
In one well-known study, participants who were given a coffee mug demanded, on average, about twice as much to sell it as other participants were willing to pay to acquire one.
Researchers call this gap the endowment effect and commonly attribute it to loss aversion: giving up something one owns is felt as a loss, and losses loom larger than equivalent gains.
Some economists have objected that the effect is an artifact of inexperience, since professional traders, who buy and sell constantly, show little of it.
But that objection may confirm rather than undermine the explanation, for traders typically acquire goods intending to sell them and so may never regard those goods as their own.

questions.prompt: The author mentions professional traders primarily in order to

options.t: show that loss aversion is strongest among experienced people
options.why: The passage suggests the opposite.

options.t: explain how the coffee mug study was designed
options.why: Traders are unrelated to the mug study's design.

options.t: present an objection and then suggest that it is consistent with the author's explanation
options.why: The objection is stated, then turned around with "may confirm rather than undermine."

options.t: provide further evidence that the endowment effect occurs in everyone
options.why: Traders show little of the effect.

options.t: argue that standard economic theory is correct after all
options.why: The author does not defend standard theory.

questions.explain: Function questions ask why something is there. Here the traders appear as part of an objection, which the author then answers.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, the endowment effect refers to

options.t: the assumption that ownership does not affect value
options.why: That is standard theory, which the effect contradicts.

options.t: the tendency of people to buy objects they do not need
options.why: Not mentioned.

options.t: the greater satisfaction people feel from gains than from losses
options.why: This reverses loss aversion.

options.t: the habit of professional traders to sell goods quickly
options.why: Not mentioned.

options.t: the difference between the price owners demand and the price nonowners will pay
options.why: The passage calls "this gap" the endowment effect.

questions.explain: For detail questions, find the defining line. "Researchers call this gap the endowment effect" points back to the gap between selling and buying prices.

questions.prompt: The author's reply to the economists' objection depends on which of the following?

options.t: Professional traders are less rational than other people.
options.why: The reply does not depend on this.

options.t: Loss aversion applies only to things a person regards as his or her own.
options.why: If traders do not feel ownership, they feel no loss, so the explanation survives.

options.t: Whether a person regards an object as his or her own can depend on why it was acquired.
options.why: The reply turns on traders acquiring goods "intending to sell them."

questions.explain: Ask what must be true for the reply to work. It needs ownership feelings to drive loss aversion, and it needs the purpose of acquisition to affect those feelings.

title: Seeing planets by their shadows
paras: Most of the planets so far detected outside our solar system were found by the transit method, which looks for the slight, periodic dimming of a star as a planet passes in front of it.
The method is powerful but biased.
A transit can be seen only if the planet's orbit is aligned almost edge-on to our line of sight, and the chance of such an alignment falls sharply as the distance between planet and star grows.
Large planets, moreover, block more light than small ones and so produce signals that are easier to distinguish from the star's natural flickering.
It is therefore unsurprising that early transit surveys turned up many hot Jupiters, giant planets orbiting very close to their stars.
Their abundance in the catalogs says more about the method than about the galaxy.

questions.prompt: The final sentence of the passage suggests that

options.t: the transit method cannot detect planets that are far from their stars
options.why: The chance "falls sharply," which is not the same as impossible.

options.t: stars with hot Jupiters flicker more than other stars
options.why: Not stated.

options.t: the number of hot Jupiters in catalogs may not reflect how common they actually are
options.why: The catalogs reflect what the method can see, not what exists.

options.t: astronomers should stop using the transit method
options.why: The passage calls the method powerful.

options.t: hot Jupiters are the most common type of planet in the galaxy
options.why: This is the conclusion the sentence warns against.

questions.explain: "Says more about the method than about the galaxy" means the result reflects a detection bias. Avoid answers that overstate it.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which of the following make a planet more likely to be detected by the transit method?

options.t: a large size
options.why: Large planets block more light and produce clearer signals.

options.t: a short distance from its star
options.why: Edge-on alignment is more likely for close planets.

options.t: a star that flickers strongly
options.why: Strong flickering makes signals harder to distinguish.

questions.explain: Two factors are named in the passage. The third choice is a factor too, but it works in the opposite direction.

questions.prompt: Select the sentence that states the author's overall judgment of the transit method.
questions.explain: The rest of the passage explains and illustrates this short sentence, which is the thesis.

title: Novels in installments
paras: Many Victorian novels first reached readers not as books but in monthly or weekly installments, and critics have long argued that this mode of publication shaped the novels themselves.

Because each installment had to sell the next, authors ended parts on moments of suspense, multiplied subplots that could be advanced in turn, and created memorable minor characters whose return readers would anticipate.
Dickens, who published nearly all his novels this way, also adjusted stories in response to sales; when the early numbers of Martin Chuzzlewit sold poorly, he abruptly sent his hero to America.
To modern readers, the resulting looseness of structure can look like a flaw.
It might be better understood as the signature of a form designed for an audience that read slowly, over many months, and often aloud in company.

questions.prompt: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.t: explaining how a publishing practice shaped novels and suggesting a different way to judge them
options.why: Covers the influence of serialization and the closing reassessment.

options.t: criticizing Victorian novelists for writing loosely structured books
options.why: The author defends the looseness.

options.t: describing the reading habits of Victorian audiences
options.why: These appear only in the final sentence.

options.t: arguing that Dickens was the most commercially minded Victorian novelist
options.why: No such comparison is made.

options.t: comparing serialized novels with novels published as complete books
options.why: No comparison is made.

questions.explain: The last two sentences turn from description to evaluation. A purpose answer must include both the explanation and the reassessment.

questions.prompt: The reference to Martin Chuzzlewit serves primarily to

options.t: contradict the critics mentioned in the first sentence
options.why: It supports their claim.

options.t: suggest that serialized novels were usually set abroad
options.why: Not implied.

options.t: provide an example of a memorable minor character
options.why: The example concerns the hero's plot, not a minor character.

options.t: show that Dickens's novels were generally unpopular
options.why: Only the early numbers of one novel sold poorly.

options.t: illustrate how commercial pressure could alter the course of a novel
options.why: Poor sales led Dickens to change the plot.

questions.explain: Ask what point the example proves. It shows the story bending to sales, which supports the claim that serialization shaped novels.

questions.prompt: Select the sentence in which the author proposes an alternative to a common judgment.
questions.explain: The sentence before states the common judgment ("can look like a flaw"); this sentence offers the alternative.

title: Bicycle lanes
paras: In the two years after the city of Harwell painted bicycle lanes on its main streets, the number of reported collisions between cars and bicycles rose by thirty percent.
A city councilor concludes that the lanes have made cycling in Harwell more dangerous and should be removed.

questions.prompt: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the councilor's conclusion?

options.t: The lanes cost less to install than the city had projected.
options.why: Cost is irrelevant to safety.

options.t: The number of people cycling in Harwell more than doubled after the lanes were painted.
options.why: With twice as many cyclists, a 30 percent rise in collisions means the risk per cyclist fell.

options.t: Most of the collisions occurred on weekday mornings.
options.why: Timing says nothing about whether cycling became more dangerous.

options.t: Some cyclists in Harwell ride outside the painted lanes.
options.why: This does not show the lanes are safe or unsafe.

options.t: Collisions between cars and pedestrians also rose in Harwell.
options.why: This does not address cyclists.

questions.explain: The councilor treats a rise in the number of collisions as a rise in danger. Danger is a rate, so more cyclists offer an alternative explanation.

questions.prompt: The councilor's argument assumes which of the following?

options.t: Bicycle lanes are cheaper to remove than to maintain.
options.why: The argument is about safety, not cost.

options.t: The increase in collisions was not due mainly to an increase in the number of cyclists.
options.why: Negate it: if more cyclists caused the rise, the conclusion fails.

options.t: Collisions between cars and bicycles are more common than collisions between cars.
options.why: Irrelevant.

options.t: No collisions occurred inside the lanes themselves.
options.why: The argument does not need this.

options.t: Cyclists prefer streets that have bicycle lanes.
options.why: Not required.

questions.explain: Use the negation test. Only one choice, when negated, destroys the argument.

title: Rethinking the guilds
paras: For much of the twentieth century, historians portrayed the craft guilds of medieval Europe as obstacles to progress.

Guilds restricted entry into trades, fixed prices, and enforced detailed rules about how goods were to be made; such controls, the argument ran, protected established masters at the expense of consumers and smothered innovation.
More recent scholarship has complicated this picture.

Some economic historians point out that the long apprenticeships guilds required were an efficient way to transmit skills that could not easily be written down, and that guild regulations assured buyers of a product's quality at a time when buyers had few other ways to judge it.
The revisionists have not, however, simply reversed the older verdict.
Even sympathetic scholars concede that guilds often resisted techniques that threatened their members' livelihoods, as when some weavers' guilds opposed the spread of mechanized fulling mills.
What has changed is the question being asked.

Rather than whether guilds helped or hindered the economy, historians now ask under what conditions they did each, a shift that has made the institution look less like a single obstacle than like a tool whose effects depended on its users.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.t: Recent historians have shown that guilds encouraged innovation.
options.why: The passage notes guilds resisted some innovations.

options.t: Guilds were chiefly responsible for transmitting technical skills in medieval Europe.
options.why: Overstates one detail.

options.t: Guilds were more beneficial to medieval economies than historians once believed.
options.why: Partly true, but it ignores that revisionists did not reverse the verdict.

options.t: Historians' view of guilds has moved from a uniformly negative judgment toward one in which their effects depended on circumstances.
options.why: Captures both the shift and its limits.

options.t: The fulling mill was the most important technology opposed by guilds.
options.why: The mill is only an example.

questions.explain: Trap A is "half right." The second paragraph says the revisionists did not simply reverse the older view, so the main idea is a change in the question, not a reversal.

questions.prompt: The first sentence of the second paragraph serves primarily to

options.t: summarize the argument of the economic historians
options.why: It limits that argument rather than summarizing it.

options.t: restate the twentieth-century view of guilds
options.why: It does not restate that view.

options.t: suggest that the older verdict was correct after all
options.why: Too strong.

options.t: qualify the account of recent scholarship given in the first paragraph
options.why: It warns against reading the revision as a full reversal.

options.t: introduce evidence that contradicts the revisionists
options.why: The evidence that follows is something revisionists themselves concede.

questions.explain: "Not, however, simply..." is a qualifying move. Look for an answer that limits, not one that reverses.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which of the following have been cited in support of a more favorable view of guilds?

options.t: Apprenticeships transmitted skills that were hard to write down.
options.why: Stated directly.

options.t: Regulations helped buyers judge the quality of goods.
options.why: Stated directly.

options.t: Guilds lowered prices for consumers.
options.why: Guilds fixed prices; lower prices are never claimed.

questions.explain: Both supported choices come from the economic historians' sentence. The third sounds positive but is not in the passage.

questions.prompt: Select the sentence that specifies the question historians now ask about guilds.
questions.explain: The sentence before announces that the question changed; this one states what the new question is.

title: A frozen planet
paras: The Snowball Earth hypothesis holds that, roughly 700 million years ago, ice sheets advanced from the poles to the equator, encasing nearly the entire planet.
The idea first seemed absurd, partly because it appeared to contain a trap: once ice covered the globe, its bright surface would reflect so much sunlight that the planet could never warm again.

Proponents answered that volcanoes would continue to emit carbon dioxide, and that with oceans sealed beneath ice and rocks no longer exposed to rain, the processes that ordinarily remove the gas from the air would largely stop.
Over millions of years, carbon dioxide would accumulate until the greenhouse effect overwhelmed the ice.
This account explained a puzzling feature of the geological record: thick layers of carbonate rock, which typically form in warm seas, lying directly on top of glacial deposits.
If the hypothesis is right, the carbonates record the sudden, hot aftermath of the freeze, when vast amounts of carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans.
Critics continue to argue that some open water must have persisted near the equator, but even they concede that the glaciations were far more extensive than any in the planet's later history.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, the hypothesis at first seemed absurd partly because

options.t: carbonate rock cannot form in cold seas
options.why: This fact supports the hypothesis, not the doubts.

options.t: volcanoes could not have erupted beneath the ice
options.why: Volcanoes are part of the proponents' answer.

options.t: ice sheets cannot reach the equator because the sunlight there is too strong
options.why: Plausible, but not in the passage.

options.t: the early atmosphere contained too little carbon dioxide
options.why: Not stated.

options.t: a fully frozen planet seemed unable ever to escape its frozen state
options.why: This is the "trap" the passage describes.

questions.explain: Locate the word "absurd" and read the rest of that sentence. The reason follows the colon.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred that, under ordinary conditions, carbon dioxide is removed from the atmosphere partly through processes involving

options.t: the reflection of sunlight by ice
options.why: Unrelated to removing the gas.

options.t: rain falling on exposed rock
options.why: The removal processes stop when rocks are "no longer exposed to rain."

options.t: the cooling of the oceans
options.why: Not mentioned.

options.t: volcanic eruptions
options.why: Volcanoes add carbon dioxide.

options.t: the formation of glacial deposits
options.why: Not mentioned as a removal process.

questions.explain: The passage says removal stops when rocks are not exposed to rain, which implies that rain on exposed rock is part of how removal normally happens.

questions.prompt: The discussion of carbonate rock in the second paragraph serves primarily to

options.t: show that the glaciations were less extensive than proponents claim
options.why: Not its role.

options.t: present evidence that the hypothesis can account for
options.why: "This account explained a puzzling feature."

options.t: describe how glacial deposits form
options.why: Not described.

options.t: explain why critics believe open water persisted
options.why: The critics' view comes later and is separate.

options.t: challenge the proponents' explanation of how the planet warmed
options.why: It supports that explanation.

questions.explain: The paragraph begins "This account explained..." The carbonates are a puzzle that the hypothesis solves.

questions.prompt: Select the sentence that indicates a point on which critics and proponents of the hypothesis agree.
questions.explain: "Even they concede" marks common ground: the glaciations were unusually extensive.

title: The strength of weak ties
paras: In a study of how people in a Boston suburb had found their jobs, the sociologist Mark Granovetter noticed something surprising: those who had learned of their positions through personal contacts had more often heard about them from acquaintances than from close friends.
He proposed an explanation that has since become one of the most cited ideas in the social sciences.
Close friends tend to know one another and to move in the same circles, so the information that reaches one usually reaches all.
Acquaintances, by contrast, connect a person to circles he or she would not otherwise touch, and so carry news that is genuinely new.
Granovetter called this the strength of weak ties.
The argument does not claim that weak ties are more valuable than strong ones in every respect.
Close friends may be more willing to help, and a recommendation from someone who knows a candidate well may count for more.
The claim is narrower: for the specific task of discovering opportunities, the breadth of a network can matter more than its depth.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?

options.t: People with many close friends rarely find jobs through personal contacts.
options.why: Not stated.

options.t: Granovetter's study has been widely criticized.
options.why: The passage says it is widely cited.

options.t: Close friends are less helpful than acquaintances in most situations.
options.why: The second paragraph explicitly rejects this.

options.t: Information spreads faster among acquaintances than among friends.
options.why: The point is that acquaintances bring new information, not faster information.

options.t: Loose social connections can be especially useful for learning about opportunities, because they link people to otherwise separate groups.
options.why: States the claim and the reason, and keeps its narrow scope.

questions.explain: The second paragraph exists to narrow the claim. A correct main idea respects that narrow scope.

questions.prompt: Which of the following situations best illustrates the principle described in the passage?

options.t: An employer hires a candidate whom a trusted friend knows well.
options.why: Depth of a tie, not breadth.

options.t: A student hears about a scholarship from three of her roommates at once.
options.why: Close ties sharing the same information.

options.t: A relative lends a job seeker money while he looks for work.
options.why: Help, not information.

options.t: A man learns of an opening at a distant firm from a former classmate he sees once a year.
options.why: A weak tie brings information from another circle.

options.t: A woman is promoted after her closest colleague recommends her.
options.why: A strong tie giving help, not news.

questions.explain: First name the principle: weak ties bring new information from other circles. Then find the option with that structure.

questions.prompt: The second paragraph suggests which of the following?

options.t: Recommendations from acquaintances count for more than those from friends.
options.why: The passage suggests the opposite.

options.t: Strong ties may offer advantages that weak ties do not.
options.why: Friends may be more willing to help.

options.t: The value of a social connection depends partly on what it is being used for.
options.why: "For the specific task of discovering opportunities."

questions.explain: The paragraph limits the claim to one task, which implies that other tasks may favor strong ties.

title: A surprising year at the theater
paras: Last year the Cartwell Theater raised its ticket prices by twenty percent, yet the number of tickets it sold also rose.
Over the same period, ticket prices at the only other theater in town did not change.
The Cartwell's manager concludes that customers took the higher prices as a sign of higher quality.

questions.prompt: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain how the Cartwell sold more tickets despite raising its prices?

options.t: Last year the Cartwell began staging productions by a popular touring company, while the other theater's programming did not change.
options.why: A new attraction raised demand enough to outweigh higher prices.

options.t: The cost of staging productions rose at both theaters.
options.why: Explains a price rise, not higher sales.

options.t: The Cartwell advertised less last year than in previous years.
options.why: This makes the result more puzzling.

options.t: Most people who attend the Cartwell also attend the other theater.
options.why: Does not explain the rise.

options.t: Ticket prices at the Cartwell had been unchanged for several years.
options.why: Does not explain why sales rose.

questions.explain: A paradox answer lets both facts be true at once: higher prices and higher sales. Something else must have increased demand.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the manager's conclusion?

options.t: How many seats the other theater has
options.why: Irrelevant to the cause.

options.t: Whether the Cartwell changed anything other than its prices last year
options.why: If something else changed, it may explain the sales rise instead.

options.t: Whether theaters in other towns raised their prices
options.why: Does not test the manager's explanation.

options.t: What percentage of tickets were sold online
options.why: Irrelevant.

options.t: Whether the Cartwell plans to raise prices again
options.why: About the future, not the cause.

questions.explain: The manager picks one cause. The most useful question checks for other causes.

title: Keystones and arches
paras: In 1969 the ecologist Robert Paine introduced the term keystone species to describe a predator whose influence on its community is far larger than its abundance would suggest.

Paine had removed a starfish, Pisaster ochraceus, from stretches of the rocky shore of Washington State and watched as mussels, freed from their chief predator, crowded out nearly every other species; diversity in the experimental plots collapsed.
A few years later, studies of the Pacific coast supplied what became the most famous example.
Where sea otters were abundant, they kept sea urchins in check, and forests of kelp flourished; where otters had been hunted out, urchins multiplied and grazed the kelp down to barren rock.
The removal of a single species, it seemed, could unravel an ecosystem.
The concept proved enormously influential, not least because it offered conservationists a strategy.
If certain species hold communities together, protecting them might protect much else besides.
Yet as the term spread, its meaning grew loose.
Researchers applied it to herbivores, to plants, even to organisms whose importance rested on their sheer numbers, the very situation Paine's definition had been meant to exclude.
Some ecologists began to argue that a label applied so widely had ceased to identify anything in particular.
A further difficulty is that keystone status may not be a fixed property of a species at all.
In some places, kelp forests seem to depend less on otters than on water temperature and the supply of nutrients.
Paine's starfish, too, matters far less on stretches of shore where mussels are scarce to begin with.
Such findings suggest that the same species may be central in one setting and marginal in another, and that the question of whether a species is a keystone is incomplete unless one also asks where.

Defenders of the concept reply that this dependence on context does not undermine the idea so much as specify it, much as the importance of a stone in an arch depends on where in the arch it is placed.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.t: describe Paine's experiments in detail
options.why: They occupy only part of the first paragraph.

options.t: defend the keystone concept against its critics
options.why: The passage presents both critics and defenders.

options.t: propose a new definition of keystone species
options.why: No new definition is proposed.

options.t: argue that sea otters matter more than starfish
options.why: No such comparison.

options.t: trace the development of an ecological concept and discuss challenges to it
options.why: Origin, spread, and two problems.

questions.explain: Map the paragraphs: origin, spread and loosening, dependence on place. The purpose answer must cover that whole arc.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred that Paine's original definition would NOT apply to

options.t: a species whose influence varies from place to place
options.why: The definition does not exclude this.

options.t: a species that shapes its community chiefly because it is extremely numerous
options.why: "The very situation Paine's definition had been meant to exclude."

options.t: a species that is uncommon but has large effects
options.why: That is the definition.

options.t: a starfish that preys on mussels
options.why: That was Paine's own example.

options.t: a predator whose removal causes a sharp decline in diversity
options.why: That fits the definition.

questions.explain: Note the word NOT. The passage names one situation the definition was meant to exclude: importance based on sheer numbers.

questions.prompt: The reference to a stone in an arch serves primarily to

options.t: show that keystone species are always predators
options.why: Not addressed.

options.t: illustrate the critics' claim that the concept is too vague
options.why: The analogy belongs to the defenders.

options.t: suggest that ecosystems are as stable as buildings
options.why: Not the point.

options.t: explain why conservationists favor the concept
options.why: That was the second paragraph's topic.

options.t: support the view that a species' importance can depend on its position within a particular system
options.why: A stone matters according to where it sits.

questions.explain: Who uses the analogy, and for what? Defenders use it to argue that context specifies the concept rather than undermining it.

questions.prompt: Which of the following does the passage present as difficulties for the keystone concept?

options.t: Removing a keystone species has rarely had measurable effects.
options.why: The passage gives examples where it had large effects.

options.t: The term has been applied so broadly that it may no longer identify a distinct kind of species.
options.why: Second paragraph.

options.t: A species may play a central role in some places but not in others.
options.why: Third paragraph.

questions.explain: Each correct choice matches one paragraph's problem. The wrong one contradicts the first paragraph.

questions.prompt: Select the sentence that describes the strategy the concept offered to conservationists.
questions.explain: The sentence before says the concept offered a strategy; this one states what the strategy was.

title: Is improvisation composition?
paras: It is often said that improvisation is composition in real time, and the phrase captures something true.
A jazz soloist, like a composer, creates melodies, shapes them into larger designs, and makes choices about harmony and rhythm.
Yet the comparison can mislead if it suggests that the improviser simply does quickly what the composer does slowly.
The conditions under which the two work differ in kind, not merely in speed.
A composer can revise.
A passage that does not work can be crossed out, and the finished score presents only the choices that survived.
The improviser's choices, by contrast, cannot be taken back once they sound.
A note that seems wrong cannot be withdrawn; it can only be redeemed by what follows, and accomplished improvisers are known for turning apparent errors into the seeds of new ideas.
Improvisation is therefore less like writing than like conversation, in which meaning emerges from a sequence of commitments that each speaker must honor and build upon.
This difference helps explain why improvisers rely heavily on what musicians call vocabulary: stock phrases, practiced so often that they can be summoned without deliberation.
Critics have sometimes treated such phrases as evidence that improvisation is less creative than its admirers claim.
But fluency in a language does not consist in inventing new words; it consists in combining familiar ones in ways suited to the moment.

The improviser's originality, on this view, lies less in the material than in its arrangement and timing, in the response, often within a fraction of a second, to what the other players have just done.

To judge improvisation by the standards of written composition is thus to misjudge it, much as one would misjudge a brilliant conversationalist by asking whether her remarks would read well as an essay.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.t: Although improvisation resembles composition, it works under different conditions and should be judged by different standards.
options.why: Covers the resemblance, the difference, and the conclusion.

options.t: Improvisation is a less demanding form of composition.
options.why: The author argues it is a different activity, not a lesser one.

options.t: Jazz soloists rely too heavily on stock phrases.
options.why: This is the critics' view, which the author rejects.

options.t: Composers should learn to improvise in order to write better music.
options.why: Not discussed.

options.t: Music and conversation share the same structure.
options.why: Overstated; conversation is an analogy.

questions.explain: The first paragraph sets up "resembles but differs," and the last sentence draws the conclusion about judging. Both must be in the answer.

questions.prompt: The author's attitude toward the phrase "composition in real time" is best described as

options.t: amusement at its popularity
options.why: No such tone.

options.t: acceptance of it as partly accurate but potentially misleading
options.why: "Captures something true... Yet the comparison can mislead."

options.t: complete rejection
options.why: The author says it "captures something true."

options.t: indifference
options.why: The whole passage responds to it.

options.t: unqualified endorsement
options.why: The author qualifies it.

questions.explain: Again, look for the qualifier. "Something true" plus "can mislead" points to a balanced attitude.

questions.prompt: The second paragraph primarily serves to

options.t: show that conversation is a form of music
options.why: The analogy runs the other way and is only a comparison.

options.t: describe how improvisers learn stock phrases
options.why: That is the third paragraph.

options.t: identify a specific difference between the conditions in which composers and improvisers work
options.why: Revision versus choices that cannot be taken back.

options.t: give an example of a famous improvised error
options.why: No specific example is given.

options.t: argue that composers are more careful than improvisers
options.why: Not a judgment of care.

questions.explain: The first paragraph claims the conditions "differ in kind." The second paragraph supplies the difference.

questions.prompt: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.t: A musician who uses many practiced phrases can still be highly original.
options.why: Originality lies in arrangement and timing.

options.t: Responding to the other players is part of what makes improvisation creative.
options.why: "In the response... to what the other players have just done."

options.t: The best improvisers rarely play notes that seem wrong.
options.why: The author says they redeem such notes, not avoid them.

questions.explain: Check each claim against a specific line. B sounds sensible but is not what the passage says about errors.

title: The drift of continents
paras: When Alfred Wegener proposed in 1912 that the continents had once formed a single landmass and had since drifted apart, he assembled an impressive body of evidence.

The coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like puzzle pieces; fossils of the same ancient reptiles appeared on continents now separated by oceans; and rock formations and traces of ancient glaciers lined up across the Atlantic when the continents were reassembled.

Yet for nearly half a century most geologists rejected the theory, and the story of its eventual triumph is often told as a parable of scientific conservatism, of an establishment too attached to its assumptions to recognize a visionary.
That telling is not entirely fair.
The chief objection to Wegener's theory was not that the continents could not have moved but that he could not explain how they moved.
Wegener suggested that continents plowed through the ocean floor, driven by forces arising from the Earth's rotation, and physicists showed that these forces were far too weak.
For his critics, a theory that described an effect without a plausible cause was not yet a scientific explanation.
One may think this standard too strict, but it was not unreasonable.
What changed opinion in the 1960s was not a rediscovery of Wegener's evidence but new evidence of a different kind.
Surveys of the ocean floor revealed long volcanic ridges, and magnetic measurements showed stripes of rock with alternating magnetic orientation arranged symmetrically on either side of them.
These patterns indicated that new crust was forming at the ridges and spreading outward, carrying the continents with it.

Plate tectonics, as the revised theory came to be called, supplied the mechanism Wegener had lacked; it also showed that his specific proposal, continents plowing through a passive ocean floor, had been wrong.
The episode thus illustrates less the blindness of the scientific community than the difference between being right about what happened and being right about why.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.t: explain the physics of seafloor spreading
options.why: Only part of the third paragraph.

options.t: celebrate Wegener as a visionary ignored by his peers
options.why: The author challenges this telling.

options.t: argue that early twentieth-century geologists were too conservative
options.why: The author argues the opposite.

options.t: show that Wegener's evidence was weaker than usually believed
options.why: The author calls it impressive.

options.t: give a more balanced account of why a theory was first rejected and later accepted
options.why: Corrects the usual story with reasons on both sides.

questions.explain: "That telling is not entirely fair" is the pivot. The author is correcting a popular story.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, the main reason geologists rejected Wegener's theory was that

options.t: he could not supply a plausible mechanism for the continents' motion
options.why: "He could not explain how they moved."

options.t: his theory conflicted with evidence of ancient glaciers
options.why: The glacier evidence supported him.

options.t: his fossil evidence was unconvincing
options.why: His evidence is called impressive.

options.t: physicists proved that continents cannot move
options.why: Physicists showed his proposed forces were too weak, which is a narrower claim.

options.t: the coastlines did not in fact fit together
options.why: Contradicted by the passage.

questions.explain: Trap D is the classic distortion: it makes the physicists' finding much broader than it was.

questions.prompt: The author regards the critics' standard for a scientific explanation as

options.t: an example of scientific conservatism
options.why: The author resists this reading.

options.t: the only correct standard
options.why: The author allows it may be "too strict."

options.t: the main reason plate tectonics was later accepted
options.why: Plate tectonics won through new evidence.

options.t: defensible, even if arguably too demanding
options.why: "One may think this standard too strict, but it was not unreasonable."

options.t: absurd
options.why: "Not unreasonable."

questions.explain: Read the sentence with "but." What follows "but" is the author's actual view.

questions.prompt: Which of the following does the passage indicate about plate tectonics?

options.t: It relied mainly on a re-examination of Wegener's evidence.
options.why: "Not a rediscovery of Wegener's evidence."

options.t: It showed that Wegener's account of how continents move was incorrect.
options.why: His "specific proposal... had been wrong."

options.t: It provided a mechanism for the movement of continents.
options.why: "Supplied the mechanism Wegener had lacked."

questions.explain: Two choices are stated in one sentence. The third contradicts the opening of the paragraph.

questions.prompt: Select the sentence that states the general lesson the author draws from the episode.
questions.explain: "Thus" signals the conclusion, which generalizes beyond Wegener.

title: Working from home
paras: A survey of employees at Dalton Software found that those who worked from home completed fifteen percent more tasks per week than those who worked in the office.
Dalton's executives conclude that requiring all employees to work from home would increase the company's productivity.

questions.prompt: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the executives' conclusion?

options.t: Some tasks at Dalton take longer to complete than others.
options.why: Says nothing about how tasks were split between the groups.

options.t: Employees who chose to work from home were, on average, more experienced than those who chose to work in the office.
options.why: The difference may come from experience, not location.

options.t: Many Dalton employees say they would prefer to work from home.
options.why: Preference is not productivity.

options.t: Dalton's competitors have not adopted work-from-home policies.
options.why: Irrelevant.

options.t: Working from home reduces employees' commuting costs.
options.why: Irrelevant to tasks completed.

questions.explain: The groups chose where to work, so they may differ in other ways. An alternative cause for the difference weakens the conclusion.

questions.prompt: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the executives' conclusion?

options.t: Employees who switched from office work to home work during the survey period completed more tasks after switching than before.
options.why: Same people, different location: this rules out differences between the groups.

options.t: Dalton's office building is expensive to maintain.
options.why: About cost, not productivity.

options.t: The survey was conducted during the company's busiest season.
options.why: Does not favor either group.

options.t: Employees who work from home report higher job satisfaction.
options.why: Satisfaction is not output.

options.t: Some office workers already work from home one day a week.
options.why: Does not support the conclusion.

questions.explain: The best strengthener rules out the main alternative explanation. Comparing the same people before and after does that.

title: The price of farming
paras: For a long time the adoption of agriculture was regarded as an unambiguous advance.

Farming, it was assumed, freed people from the uncertainties of hunting and gathering, provided a more reliable food supply, and created the surplus that made towns, writing, and specialized professions possible.
The last of these claims remains largely uncontested.
The first two have fared less well.
Studies of skeletons from many regions where farming replaced foraging have found that the transition was often followed by a decline in health.

Early farmers tended to be shorter than the foragers who preceded them, and their bones and teeth more often show signs of malnutrition and disease, including defects in tooth enamel that form when a child's growth is interrupted by illness or hunger.
Several factors may explain the pattern.

Foragers typically ate a wide variety of plants and animals, whereas farmers often relied heavily on a few starchy crops; settled communities, by concentrating people and their waste, allowed infections to spread; and a diet dependent on a few crops exposed whole communities to famine when those crops failed.
If farming made many people less healthy, why did it spread?
One answer is that its advantages lay at the level of the group rather than the individual.

Farming could support far more people per square mile than foraging, and larger populations could outnumber and displace their neighbors, regardless of whether any particular farmer was better off than any particular forager.
On this view, agriculture prevailed not because it improved lives but because it multiplied them.
Some researchers caution that the skeletal evidence is uneven and that in certain regions health improved with farming; the pattern, they argue, is a tendency rather than a law.
Even so, the older picture of agriculture as a simple step upward has become difficult to sustain.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?

options.t: The skeletal evidence is too uneven to support any conclusion.
options.why: Overstates the caution in the last paragraph.

options.t: The view of agriculture as a clear improvement has been challenged by evidence that it often worsened health, and its spread may reflect advantages for groups rather than individuals.
options.why: Covers both the evidence and the explanation.

options.t: Agriculture led to the decline of towns.
options.why: The passage says it made towns possible.

options.t: Agriculture spread because it improved the health of individuals.
options.why: The passage argues the opposite.

options.t: Foragers were healthier than people living today.
options.why: Never compared.

questions.explain: Long passages often have a two-part main idea. Choose the answer that includes both the challenge and the proposed explanation.

questions.prompt: Which of the traditional claims about agriculture does the author treat as still largely accepted?

options.t: that farming improved human health
options.why: Not one of the three traditional claims, and contradicted.

options.t: that farming provided a more reliable food supply
options.why: Has "fared less well."

options.t: that farming reduced the spread of disease
options.why: The passage says settlement helped infections spread.

options.t: that farming created a surplus that made towns and specialized professions possible
options.why: "The last of these claims remains largely uncontested."

options.t: that farming freed people from uncertainty
options.why: Has "fared less well."

questions.explain: "The last of these" points back to the third item in the list. Track list order carefully.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which of the following may have contributed to poorer health among early farmers?

options.t: a less varied diet
options.why: Reliance on a few starchy crops.

options.t: the spread of infection in settled communities
options.why: Concentrated people and waste.

options.t: a decline in population size
options.why: Farming increased population.

questions.explain: Two causes are listed in the passage. The third reverses a fact from the final paragraph.

questions.prompt: The statement that agriculture "prevailed not because it improved lives but because it multiplied them" suggests that agriculture spread mainly because

options.t: farmers lived longer than foragers
options.why: The passage suggests farmers were often less healthy.

options.t: foragers adopted farming after observing its benefits
options.why: Not suggested.

options.t: farming reduced the number of famines
options.why: It increased exposure to famine.

options.t: towns protected people from disease
options.why: Settlement helped disease spread.

options.t: farming communities grew larger and could displace foraging groups
options.why: The group-level advantage of numbers.

questions.explain: "Multiplied them" refers to population. Connect it to the sentence before, about outnumbering neighbors.

questions.prompt: Select the sentence that qualifies the evidence supporting the author's main claim.
questions.explain: "Caution," "uneven," and "a tendency rather than a law" all limit the strength of the evidence.

title: Why banks run
paras: A bank's business rests on an imbalance.
Depositors may withdraw their money at any time, but the bank lends most of that money out in loans that cannot be called back quickly.
Ordinarily this causes no trouble, because only a small fraction of depositors want their money on any given day.
But if depositors come to fear that the bank will fail, each has reason to withdraw before the others do, and the rush to withdraw can bring down even a bank that was sound to begin with.
The danger lies in the fact that such fear can fulfill itself: a run requires no real weakness, only the belief that others will run.
Deposit insurance, introduced in the United States in 1934 after thousands of banks failed in the early years of the Great Depression, addressed this danger directly.
If depositors know they will be repaid even if their bank fails, they have no reason to run, and the panic never starts.
By this measure the policy was a remarkable success: runs by insured depositors became rare.
The policy also created a new problem.
Because insured depositors no longer had reason to watch how their bank used their money, banks could take larger risks without losing deposits.
Economists call this kind of effect moral hazard: protection against a danger can encourage the behavior that makes the danger more likely.
Regulators have responded by limiting the size of insured deposits, requiring banks to hold reserves of their own capital, and examining their loans.
None of these measures restores the discipline that anxious depositors once supplied, but together they attempt to substitute the vigilance of regulators for that of customers.
Whether that substitution succeeds is a question each financial crisis has reopened.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.t: show that bank runs happen only to weak banks
options.why: The passage says sound banks can fail too.

options.t: explain how a policy removed one danger and how it gave rise to another
options.why: Runs, insurance, then moral hazard.

options.t: describe the causes of the Great Depression
options.why: Mentioned only as background.

options.t: argue that deposit insurance should be abolished
options.why: The author does not recommend abolition.

options.t: compare banking regulation in different countries
options.why: Only the United States is discussed.

questions.explain: The three paragraphs move from problem, to solution, to the solution's side effect. The purpose answer follows the same path.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred that, before deposit insurance, depositors

options.t: rarely withdrew money from banks
options.why: Not stated.

options.t: had a reason to pay attention to the risks their banks were taking
options.why: Insurance removed that reason, so it existed before.

options.t: preferred banks that took large risks
options.why: Not suggested.

options.t: were repaid in full when their bank failed
options.why: That is what insurance later guaranteed.

options.t: were legally barred from withdrawing large sums
options.why: Not suggested.

questions.explain: If insurance meant depositors "no longer had reason to watch," then before insurance they did have that reason.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would be examples of moral hazard as the passage defines it?

options.t: A homeowner installs smoke detectors because the fire insurer requires it.
options.why: The insurance leads to safer behavior, not riskier.

options.t: A company that expects a government rescue takes on riskier investments.
options.why: Protection encourages the risk it protects against.

options.t: A driver with full car insurance becomes careless about locking the car.
options.why: Protection encourages riskier behavior.

questions.explain: Apply the definition exactly: protection that encourages the behavior making the danger more likely.

questions.prompt: Select the sentence that defines a general concept illustrated by the effects of deposit insurance.
questions.explain: The sentence names and defines moral hazard in general terms.

questions.prompt: The final sentence of the passage suggests that

options.t: whether regulation adequately substitutes for depositors' vigilance remains uncertain
options.why: Each crisis "reopens" the question.

options.t: regulators have fully replaced the discipline once supplied by depositors
options.why: The passage says no measure restores it.

options.t: depositors have become more vigilant since 1934
options.why: The opposite.

options.t: financial crises are caused by deposit insurance
options.why: Too strong.

options.t: each crisis has been followed by new deposit insurance
options.why: Not stated.

questions.explain: "A question each crisis has reopened" signals an unresolved issue, not a verdict.

title: Memories that change
paras: Memories were long thought to become fixed once they had been stored.

According to the standard account, a newly formed memory is fragile for a few hours, during which proteins must be made in the brain to stabilize it, a process called consolidation, but afterward it is permanent.
In 2000, experiments on rats challenged this view.

Researchers trained the animals to associate a tone with a mild shock, waited until the memory had consolidated, and then played the tone again while blocking protein synthesis in a region of the brain involved in fear.
The next day, the rats showed little fear of the tone.
Merely recalling the memory, it appeared, had returned it to a fragile state from which it had to be stabilized anew.
The finding, called reconsolidation, has prompted interest in treating disorders such as post-traumatic stress, in which a frightening memory remains vivid.
If recalling a memory makes it changeable, it might be possible to weaken its emotional force.

Researchers caution, however, that reconsolidation occurs only under certain conditions, which are not yet well understood, and that the same changeability raises questions about the reliability of memories that have been recalled many times.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?

options.t: Protein synthesis is unnecessary for memory.
options.why: The experiment shows it is necessary.

options.t: Reconsolidation has been shown to cure post-traumatic stress.
options.why: Only "prompted interest."

options.t: Memories become permanent within a few hours of being formed.
options.why: That is the old view the passage challenges.

options.t: Rats have better memories than was previously believed.
options.why: Not the point.

options.t: Experiments suggest that recalled memories can become unstable again, a finding with possible therapeutic uses and some limits.
options.why: Covers the finding, its promise, and the caution.

questions.explain: Eliminate answers that state the old view or exaggerate the new one.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred that the rats showed little fear of the tone because

options.t: the tone was played too softly
options.why: Not suggested.

options.t: consolidation takes longer in rats than in humans
options.why: Not discussed.

options.t: the memory, once recalled, could not be stabilized again without protein synthesis
options.why: Protein synthesis was blocked during recall.

options.t: they had forgotten the tone before it was played again
options.why: Recall is what made the memory fragile.

options.t: they had never formed the memory in the first place
options.why: The memory had already consolidated.

questions.explain: Link the experimental step (blocking protein synthesis during recall) to the explanation in the paragraph's last sentence.

questions.prompt: The researchers' caution concerns which of the following?

options.t: evidence that reconsolidation does not occur in humans
options.why: Not mentioned.

options.t: the possibility that frequently recalled memories may have changed
options.why: "Reliability of memories that have been recalled many times."

options.t: uncertainty about the conditions under which reconsolidation occurs
options.why: "Not yet well understood."

questions.explain: The caution sentence has two parts joined by "and." Each matches one correct choice.

title: More lanes, same traffic
paras: Many people believe that adding lanes to a congested highway will reduce traffic.
**Yet studies of highway expansions have repeatedly found that, within a few years, traffic on the widened roads returns to its earlier level of congestion.**
The reason is that faster travel attracts new drivers who previously avoided the road or traveled at other times.
**Building more lanes is therefore unlikely to be an effective long-term solution to congestion.**

questions.prompt: In the argument, the two portions in boldface play which of the following roles?

options.t: The first is the argument's conclusion; the second is evidence for it.
options.why: Reversed.

options.t: Both are evidence for a conclusion that is not stated.
options.why: The conclusion is stated.

options.t: The first is evidence supporting the argument's main conclusion; the second is that conclusion.
options.why: "Therefore" marks the second as the conclusion.

options.t: The first is a position the argument opposes; the second is the argument's conclusion.
options.why: The opposed position is the first sentence, not the first boldface.

options.t: The first is a prediction; the second explains why the prediction will fail.
options.why: Misreads both.

questions.explain: Label each sentence before reading the options: belief the author opposes, evidence, explanation, conclusion.

questions.prompt: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.t: Some drivers avoid highways regardless of congestion.
options.why: Does not weaken.

options.t: Many drivers on widened highways are commuters.
options.why: Does not affect the reasoning.

options.t: The studies cited examined only highways in regions whose populations grew rapidly after the expansion.
options.why: Population growth could explain the returning traffic, so the result may not apply elsewhere.

options.t: Widening a highway is expensive.
options.why: Cost is not the issue.

options.t: Public transit ridership did not change after the expansions.
options.why: Does not weaken.

questions.explain: Look for a flaw in the evidence. If the studies were from unusual regions, the general conclusion may not hold.

title: Narrators we cannot trust
paras: The term unreliable narrator, coined by the critic Wayne Booth in 1961, describes a narrator whose account of events the reader has reason to doubt.
Booth's examples ranged from narrators who lie outright to those who are simply mistaken, too naive, too self-deceived, or too limited to grasp the significance of what they report.

In each case, Booth argued, the reader detects the unreliability by perceiving a gap between the narrator's values and those of the implied author, the sensibility that seems to have shaped the work as a whole.
The reader, in effect, reads past the narrator and sides with the author behind the narrator's back.
Later critics found this account incomplete.
Booth's model, they noted, assumes that a work's norms are stable and that competent readers will agree on what they are.
Yet readers in different periods and places often disagree sharply about which narrators to trust.
A narrator whose attitudes struck one generation as admirable may strike the next as obtuse or cruel, though the work itself has not changed at all.
For these critics, unreliability is not simply a property of a text, waiting to be detected, but in part the product of an interaction between a text and the assumptions its readers bring to it.
This revision has its own risks.
If unreliability depends on readers' assumptions, it becomes hard to say that any reading is mistaken, and the concept threatens to dissolve into a record of readers' preferences.

Most critics have therefore sought a middle course, granting that cultural context shapes judgments about narrators while insisting that texts supply cues, such as contradictions between a narrator's statements and the events described, that limit which judgments are plausible.
On this view, the reader does not invent unreliability, but neither does the text dictate it.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.t: argue that readers' preferences alone determine whether a narrator is reliable
options.why: The passage treats this as a risk to avoid.

options.t: describe how a critical concept has been revised and the difficulties the revision raised
options.why: Booth, the revision, the risks, the middle course.

options.t: list examples of unreliable narrators
options.why: No specific narrators are listed.

options.t: explain why Booth coined the term
options.why: Not discussed.

options.t: defend Booth's definition against its critics
options.why: The passage presents the critics' objections fairly.

questions.explain: The three paragraphs are: original idea, revision, response to the revision. The answer must follow that development.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, Booth held that readers recognize an unreliable narrator by

options.t: consulting other readers' opinions
options.why: Not stated.

options.t: considering the period in which the work was written
options.why: That is the later critics' concern.

options.t: identifying statements that are factually false
options.why: Too narrow; Booth also included narrators who are merely mistaken.

options.t: comparing the narrator with narrators in other works
options.why: Not stated.

options.t: noticing a gap between the narrator's values and those of the implied author
options.why: Stated directly.

questions.explain: Trap D is a narrow version of the truth. Booth's narrators include liars and the mistaken, and the test is a gap in values.

questions.prompt: The later critics would most likely agree that

options.t: a work's norms stay the same across historical periods
options.why: They deny this.

options.t: readers in different centuries could reasonably reach opposite judgments about the same narrator
options.why: Readers "disagree sharply about which narrators to trust."

options.t: Booth's examples were poorly chosen
options.why: Not suggested.

options.t: the implied author is the most important element of a novel
options.why: Not their view.

options.t: texts provide no clues about a narrator's reliability
options.why: They say unreliability is "in part" interaction, not wholly.

questions.explain: Watch absolute words like "no." The later critics held a moderate view: "in part."

questions.prompt: The middle course described in the final paragraph includes which of the following claims?

options.t: Features of a text limit the range of reasonable judgments about its narrator.
options.why: Texts "supply cues... that limit which judgments are plausible."

options.t: Every reading of a narrator is equally valid.
options.why: This is the risk the middle course avoids.

options.t: Readers' cultural contexts influence their judgments of narrators.
options.why: "Granting that cultural context shapes judgments."

questions.explain: The middle course grants one point to each side. Choice C is the extreme it rejects.

questions.prompt: Select the sentence that identifies a danger in the later critics' revision.
questions.explain: "Threatens to dissolve" names the danger. The sentence before only announces that there are risks.

title: A tree or a web?
paras: Since Darwin, biologists have pictured the history of life as a tree: lineages split, and once split, they evolve independently, passing genes only from parent to offspring.
For animals and plants this picture is largely accurate.
For bacteria and archaea, which make up much of the diversity of life, it is not.

These microorganisms routinely acquire genes from unrelated organisms, by absorbing fragments of DNA from their surroundings, by receiving them from viruses, or by exchanging them directly with other cells.
The process, known as horizontal gene transfer, is one reason resistance to an antibiotic can spread rapidly among bacteria of quite different kinds.
The extent of such transfer has led some biologists to argue that the tree is the wrong image for microbial evolution altogether.
If genes move freely among lineages, then different genes in the same organism may have different histories, and a family tree built from one gene may contradict a tree built from another.
Comparisons of whole genomes have confirmed that such contradictions are common.
A web, these biologists propose, would be a more faithful picture than a tree.
Others resist abandoning the tree.

They point out that some genes, particularly those involved in the basic machinery of reading and copying DNA, appear to be transferred rarely, perhaps because they work only together with many other components and so seldom function in a foreign cell.
Trees built from such genes, they argue, still reflect a genuine history of descent, even if much of the genome has been borrowed along the way.
The disagreement is partly about evidence and partly about what a picture of evolutionary history is for: whether it should represent the descent of organisms or the movement of all their genes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?

options.t: Genes involved in copying DNA are transferred more often than other genes.
options.why: The opposite.

options.t: Antibiotic resistance spreads only through horizontal gene transfer.
options.why: "One reason," not the only one.

options.t: Horizontal gene transfer has led to debate about whether a tree adequately represents the evolutionary history of microorganisms.
options.why: Covers the cause and both sides of the debate.

options.why: The passage says it fails for microbes.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred that if horizontal gene transfer were rare among bacteria, then

options.t: the web image would become more accurate
options.why: The tree would.

options.t: bacteria would be unable to reproduce
options.why: Unrelated.

options.t: trees built from different bacterial genes would more often agree with one another
options.why: Disagreement between gene trees comes from transfer.

options.t: antibiotic resistance would spread faster
options.why: It would spread more slowly, if anything.

options.t: animals would acquire more genes from bacteria
options.why: Unrelated.

questions.explain: Reverse the cause. Transfer makes gene trees disagree, so less transfer means more agreement.

options.why: It supports keeping the tree.

options.t: show that horizontal transfer occurs in animals
options.why: Not related.

options.t: identify a basis on which some biologists defend a tree-like picture
options.why: These rarely transferred genes still record descent.

options.t: illustrate how viruses transfer genes
options.why: Not related.

options.t: explain how antibiotic resistance spreads
options.why: Not related.

questions.explain: The reference appears in the paragraph beginning "Others resist abandoning the tree," so it serves the defenders.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, bacteria can acquire genes from unrelated organisms by which of the following means?

options.t: taking up DNA fragments from their surroundings
options.why: Stated.

options.t: receiving genes from viruses
options.why: Stated.

options.t: exchanging genes directly with other cells
options.why: Stated.

questions.explain: All three can be correct. Do not assume one choice must be wrong.
